five published Kindle EPUBs print these five paths on their last page. The link is baked into files that are already built, so a broken path here cannot be fixed by editing this repo - the remedy is re-uploading five books. Nothing else in the gate ties an app route to an external published artifact, and route_ownership.json alone cannot fail when both the route and its expectation are deleted together, which is why the five paths are hardcoded in the validator.

Five published Kindle EPUBs print https://weddingpdfchecklist.com/amazon/<slug> on their last page. That hostname transposes the canonical one and is baked into files already on sale, so a host-level failure - no DNS, an invalid certificate, or the redirect losing the path - cannot be fixed by editing this repo and breaks every reader arriving from a book. validate:amazon-paths covers the five paths on the canonical host and cannot see the host the books actually print. This gate fetches all five over HTTPS on the book domain, requires a 301 to the same path on weddingchecklistpdf.com ending in a 200, and separately asserts the alias is never declared as a canonical host - a second host that renders would be a duplicate indexable copy of the whole site. It uses the canonical host as a network control so an offline machine reports UNPROVEN rather than a false red.
results.repair_evidence: proved on 2026-08-29: the gate exited 1 with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND on all five printed URLs before weddingpdfchecklist.com was attached to the Worker, and passed once attach-book-domain.mjs created the custom domain and the deployed middleware answered 301 -> 200 on each path

data/cadence/policy.json restates two numbers derived from a measured rate; nothing re-derived or asserted them, and a simulated clock on 2026-08-29 showed the stored 11/5 becoming 7/3 by 2026-09-20 while the publisher kept releasing 5 a week
results.repair_rationale: derive_capacity.mjs --check fails only when data/cadence/policy.json claims more capacity than measured throughput supports, or when new_pages_per_week no longer follows from refresh_capacity_per_week; --write is the same script re-deriving both from the same measurement, so it fixes exactly the defect the check detects.
results.repair_evidence: proved on 2026-08-29 under a simulated clock of 2026-09-20: --check exited 1 naming refresh_capacity_per_week 11 against a measured 7.68/week, --write rewrote the policy to 7/3, and --check then exited 0
